newsitem.title: USA: Dole shows grit and grace in election endgame.
newsitem.headline: Dole shows grit and grace in election endgame.

text.p: In his marathon final campaign blitz and gracious concession speech, Bob Dole showed a grit and grace that supporters have long said was there but which many voters failed to see.

As a result, a public reputation for dourness and bitterness earned in previous campaigns may give way to the image of an old soldier, battling gamely against steep odds in a last-ditch personal quest for votes for himself and his party.

"I think that he proved a lot about himself and he demonstrated tremendous courage and tremendous perseverance, and so in a personal sense I think he displayed his best qualities," Dole's spokesman, Nelson Warfield, said on Wednesday.

"In a political sense, I think that this 96-hour marathon is one of the reasons the Republicans will continue to control the House and the Senate. The energy of Senator Dole's political commitment radiated down the ballot," Warfield told reporters at Dole's campaign headquarters.
"He led the party, and the party profited from his leadership," Warfield said.
But the blitz was unable to carry the 73-year-old Dole to victory as President Bill Clinton comfortably won Tuesday's election.
In his concession speech, Dole declined to pander to the rowdies in the election-night party crowd eager for a stinging denunciation of Clinton.
"I've said repeatedly in this campaign that the president was my opponent and not my enemy," Dole said.
And he indicated that he intended to remain in public service after a 45-year career in politics.

Dole went to his campaign headquarters on Wednesday to make telephone calls and talk to aides. On his way there from his Watergate apartment, Dole said he was "feeling fine" but indicated he had left little on his agenda.
Dole has said his immediate plans were to go to his Florida condominium. His long-term plans are unclear, but Dole said in his concession speech he would remain in public life.
"I'm going to sit back for a few days, and then I'm going to start standing up for what I think is right for America," he said.
Faced with polls showing him trailing far behind Clinton, Dole set off on an unprecedented non-stop campaign tour last Friday that did not end until he arrived in Washington on Tuesday night.

"It was his idea ... a (great) way to go out," said Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain, a faithful travelling companion who has served as something of a political eulogist for Dole in the last days of the campaign. "He realised this was his last campaign and he wanted to do the best he could."

For four days and nights, fuelled by the enthusiasm of crowds, his own drive and brief cat naps, Dole soldiered on across the country seeking votes in diners, bowling alleys, airport hangars and shopping centre parking lots.
It was an grueling slog that left his voice hoarse and his entourage dazed. But it also generated one of the few periods of excitement in the campaign.
The emotional high point may have come after the first polls opened in New Hampshire and Dole watched, choked up, at a bowling alley in Des Moines as McCain spoke prophetically.

"This is the last crusade of a great warrior, a member of a generation of Americans who went out and made the world safe for democracy, so that we could have lives that were far better for ourselves and for our children," McCain said.

Asked what he learned about himself in the campaign, Dole said on Tuesday on his way back to Washington from his hometown of Russell, Kansas, "I'll think about that. Learned we got a lot of endurance."
McCain said Dole would be remembered for serving the Senate longer than any Republican leader in history, possibly to the detriment of his presidential ambitions.
"He achieved a level of trust and confidence of his colleagues that puts him up there" with greats such as Democrat Hubert Humphrey and Republican Howard Baker, McCain said.

"He really became part of the institution. It was a detriment to his presidential campaign because his whole life in the Senate was to reach conclusions that required compromise when in campaigns the whole job is to draw bright lines," McCain said.
McCain said Dole was at peace. "They're very content, he and his wife. They feel they did the best they could."
